title: What If Earth Stopped Spinning for 1 Second?
central_question: If Earth stopped spinning for one second and then started again, what would happen, and who would survive?

pronounce.1,670: one thousand six hundred and seventy
pronounce.1,180: one thousand one hundred and eighty

setting: A city street at 7:59 on a Tuesday morning; Earth from space; the South Pole. A cartoon thought experiment.
fiction_notice: A cartoon thought experiment: Earth cannot stop in one second. You, Sam and Kai are fictional; the physics numbers are real and sourced.

lines.text: This is what happens if Earth stops spinning. For one second.
And trust me, this is the nice part of town.
Let's rewind ten seconds.

badges.text: Cartoon. You and Sam are fictional

lines.text: Right now, you are moving. Fast.
Earth spins,
and at the equator the ground carries you east at about 1,670 kilometres an hour.
That's faster than the speed of sound.
Further north it's slower: about 1,180 at 45 degrees. At the poles, almost nothing.
You just turn on the spot.
So: Tuesday, 7:59 and fifty seconds. Coffee in hand.
Is that clock fast?
At eight o'clock exactly, the planet slams on the brakes.
The ground stops. You don't.

badges.text: Impossible in reality: a thought experiment

lines.text: Everything bolted to the bedrock stops with it. Buildings. Bridges. Mountains.
Everything that isn't keeps going east at full speed. People. Cars. Oceans. The air.
How hard is that stop? Going from 465 metres a second to zero in one second is about 47 g.
Fighter pilots train to survive nine. Most of us black out long before that.
Whatever is bolted down feels all of it.

badges.text: Our calculation: 465 m/s in 1 s is about 47 g

cards.title: 47 g. A fighter pilot trains for 9.

lines.text: Then the air arrives. The atmosphere doesn't stop either.
At the equator that's a wind of around 1,670 kilometres an hour.
The fastest tornado wind ever measured was about 480.
The oceans keep going too, piling up against every coast that faces east.
How big are those waves? Nobody can say for sure. Let's just say: big.

badges.text: Wave heights: nobody has modelled this

lines.text: And here's the part nobody mentions.
One second later, Earth starts spinning again. A second lurch, the other way.
One second. Two disasters.

badges.text: The restart is part of the thought experiment

lines.text: So who survives? Someone standing exactly on a pole.
Meet Kai, at the South Pole. Kai was barely moving to begin with, so Kai just... wobbles.
Huh. Anyone else spill their tea?
And no, there are no penguins to tell.
They live on the coast, about 1,400 kilometres away.

badges.text: No penguins at the Pole; nearest colony ~1,400 km

lines.text: Good news: nothing in the universe is going to stop Earth in one second.
Bad news: something is slowing it down. Right now.
The Moon.
Its tides act like a brake,
and every century the day gets a couple of milliseconds longer.
Wait about 200 million years, and you get a 25-hour day.
Finally, time to finish that coffee.

badges.text: Day lengthens ~1.8 ms per century (eclipse records)

lines.text: So. You get ten seconds' warning. Where on Earth do you run?
Tell me your city in the comments, and I'll tell you how fast you were going.
Next time: what if the Moon vanished tonight?

cards.title: Where would you run? Comment your city.

claims.text: The scenario is a cartoon thought experiment: nothing can stop Earth in one second. You, Sam and Kai, the street and the clock are fictional.
Earth's surface at the equator moves east at about 1,670 km/h (about 465 m/s); the speed falls with the cosine of latitude, to about 1,180 km/h at 45 degrees and almost zero at the poles.
The speed of sound in air at 20 degrees C is about 343 m/s, or about 1,235 km/h, so the equator's rotation speed is faster than sound.
If the ground stopped, anything not attached to it (people, vehicles, oceans, the atmosphere) would keep moving east at the rotation speed (inertia).
Our calculation: slowing from 465 m/s to zero in one second is an average deceleration of 465 m/s squared, about 47 times the 9.81 m/s squared of gravity (about 47 g).
Fighter pilots are trained to sustain about 9 g; untrained people often lose consciousness at much lower sustained g (sources vary, around 4 to 6 g).
The fastest tornado wind ever measured was about 301 mph (about 484 km/h, plus or minus 20 mph), by mobile Doppler radar in the Bridge Creek-Moore tornado of 3 May 1999.
Penguins do not live at the South Pole; they live on Antarctica's coasts. The most southern colony (Adelie penguins at Cape Royds) is about 1,400 km from the Pole.

Tidal friction from the Moon is slowing Earth's rotation: the tidal braking alone adds about 2.3 ms per century, and eclipse records show an observed average of about 1.7-1.8 ms per century; at that rate a 25-hour day is about 200 million years away.
The size of the ocean surge and the effects of the spin restarting are speculation; no source models a one-second stop and restart.

titles: What If Earth Stopped Spinning for 1 Second?
Earth Stops for 1 Second. You Don't.
The One Second That Would End the World
publishing.description: At 8:00 a.m. tomorrow, Earth stops spinning. For one second. Then it starts again. Sounds harmless? You're already moving at about 1,670 km/h, and the ground is about to stop without you. We follow one ordinary Tuesday morning through the physics: what keeps moving, how hard that stop really is, a wind faster than any tornado ever measured, the oceans, the restart nobody talks about, the one person who survives, and the real reason Earth IS slowing down right now.
publishing.whats_real: What's real: the rotation speeds, the speed of sound, inertia, the g-force calculation, the record tornado wind, where penguins live, and the Moon's slow braking of Earth's spin are sourced below. What isn't: Earth cannot stop in one second, so the scenario is a cartoon thought experiment; you, Sam and Kai are fictional; the size of the ocean surge and the restart are labelled HYPOTHETICAL on screen.
publishing.cta: You get ten seconds' warning. Where do you run? Comment your city and I'll tell you how fast you were going.
